strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper systematically studies how different levels of future information (none, normalization, frequency predictions) affect the achievability of standard fairness notions (EF1/EFX/PROP1/MMS and approximations) in online fair division, building naturally on Zhou et al. (ICML 2023) and connecting to semi-online scheduling and algorithms-with-predictions.

The headline contribution, Theorem 5.1, is genuinely interesting: a constructive meta-algorithm showing that ANY share-based fairness notion achievable offline (e.g., (3/4+3/3836)-MMS, RRS, MXS) can be achieved online given frequency predictions. The IDO-based simulation of picking sequences (Lemmas 5.2, 5.3) is a clean and novel technique, and the corollary strictly improves the 0.5-MMS guarantee of Zhou et al. for n ≥ 3.

Good coverage of complementary results: the paper pairs nearly every positive result with a matching or near-matching impossibility (e.g., no positive approximation to EF1 without information; EFX impossible with normalization even for n=2; tight (√5−1)/2-EFX with identical valuations and normalization for n=2, Theorem 6.3, whose tightness proof is careful and correct as far as I could verify).

Useful scholarly service: the paper identifies an actual error in Kahana and Hazon (2023)'s claimed PROP1 impossibility (Example 3.2), correctly diagnosing the failed induction, and honestly frames the remaining PROP1 approximation question as open.

Algorithms are precisely specified (Algorithms 1–3), the adversarial/adaptive model and multiplicative approximation conventions are clearly stated, and the related work section is thorough and well-differentiated (learning-augmented vs. advice-based settings).
weaknesses: I believe there is a gap in the proofs of Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 (the core normalization-section results). Both proofs rely on the claim that at termination every active agent has v_i(A_i) < 1/n and every inactive agent has v_i(A_i) < 1/n. This claim is false: because the inactivity test uses x_i = v_i(A_i) + ((n−1)/n)·max{...}, an agent can receive a good that pushes v_i(A_i) ≥ 1/n while x_i < 1/n, and an agent can be set inactive via the max term with v_i(A_i) ≥ 1/n. Concrete counterexample (n=2, normalized): goods in arrival order with (v_1, v_2) = (0.2, 0.2), (0.225, 0.29), (0.225, 0.29), (0.35, 0.22). Algorithm 1 outputs A_1 = {g_1, g_4} with v_1(A_1) = 0.55 ≥ 1/2 (agent 1 active at termination) and A_2 = {g_2, g_3} with v_2(A_2) = 0.58 ≥ 1/2 (agent 2 inactive with value ≥ 1/2), and Σ v_i(A_i) = 1.13 > 1, contradicting the intermediate inequalities used in both proofs. The final allocations in this instance are still EF1/PROP1, so the theorem statements may well be true, but the proofs as written are incorrect and need repair (or a modified algorithm/analysis).

Several proofs are terse and have typos that hinder verification, e.g., 'v_2(g′) ≥ v_2(g′)' in Theorem 4.1 Case 1; 'B_2 = {f(g) | g ∈ A_2 \ {f(g*)}}' should be '\{g*}' in Theorem 5.5; 'as δ → 0' should be 'δ → ∞' in Theorem 4.4 Case 2; 'Elkind Elkind' in the references; an unbalanced parenthesis in the Schiffer and Zhang entry. In a paper whose value rests on proof correctness, these should be cleaned up.

A significant portion of the impossibility results (Propositions 3.1, 6.2, Theorems 4.3, 4.4, 5.6, 6.4) are fairly standard adaptive-adversary constructions; individually they are unsurprising, so the paper's weight rests heavily on Theorem 5.1 and the Section 4 algorithm — the latter having the proof gap above.

The frequency-prediction model is strong information (exact multiset of all future values, hence exact m); the paper acknowledges but does not explore robustness to noisy predictions, which limits practical reach (though this is honestly flagged as future work).

The open problem left in Section 5 (does EF1 hold for n ≥ 3 with frequency predictions?) is a natural gap; the paper conjectures impossibility but offers no partial evidence, which slightly weakens the completeness of the Section 5 landscape.

strengths: The paper offers a systematic and well-organized treatment of how different levels of future information (none, normalization, frequency predictions, identical valuations) affect the achievability of standard fairness notions (EFX, EF1, PROP1, MMS and their approximations) in online fair division. The structural taxonomy across Sections 3-6 makes the landscape easy to navigate.

Theorem 5.1 is the most original contribution: a general meta-algorithm showing that any share-based fairness notion feasible in the single-shot setting (e.g., RRS, MXS, (3/4 + 3/3836)-MMS) can be matched online given frequency predictions. The lifting argument via IDO valuations and picking sequences (Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3) is clean, constructive, and immediately yields Corollary 5.4, which strictly improves on the tight 0.5-MMS guarantee of Zhou et al. (2023) under weaker information.

Several results are complemented by matching upper and lower bounds, e.g., the tight (sqrt(5)-1)/2-EFX guarantee for two agents with identical valuations and normalization (Theorem 6.3), which strengthens the paper's claims beyond mere existence.

The paper corrects an error in Kahana and Hazon (2023) regarding PROP1 impossibility (Example 3.2) and strengthens Benadè et al. (2018)'s EF1 impossibility to any positive approximation (Proposition 3.1), which is a genuine service to the community.

The writing is generally clear, the related work is thorough and up to date (covering learning-augmented allocation, temporal fair division, and semi-online scheduling), and the impossibility proofs use explicit valuation tables that make the adversary constructions verifiable.
weaknesses: The frequency-prediction model is a very strong information assumption: the algorithm is given the exact multiset of every agent's future valuations (and hence the exact number of goods). Under this assumption, much of the randomness of the online problem is removed, which limits the practical significance of Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.4. The paper acknowledges only in the conclusion that robustness to noisy or imperfect predictions is future work; no consistency/robustness analysis is provided, in contrast to the learning-augmented literature it positions itself against (Section 1.2).

A substantial portion of the positive results in Section 4 is an incremental modification of Zhou et al. (2023)'s algorithm (Algorithm 1 generalizes Zhou et al.'s Algorithm 1 from 0.5-MMS to EF1/PROP1), and several impossibility arguments follow the standard adversary/case-split template already used by Zhou et al. and Benadè et al. The novelty is real but modest, and the paper's framing as 'initiating' the study of EF/PROP somewhat overstates the delta over prior work.

The manuscript contains a noticeable number of proof and presentation errors that, while mostly not fatal, require careful reader repair: e.g., in Theorem 4.1 Case 1, 'for each good g' in A2, v2(g') >= v2(g')' should be v2(g') >= v1(g'); in Theorem 4.4 Case 2, the limit is written 'as delta -> 0' where it must be delta -> infinity; in Theorem 4.3, 'v1(A2) \ {g1}' is ill-formed notation; in Theorem 5.5, B2 is defined as {f(g) | g in A2 \ {f(g*)}} mixing g and f(g), and sentences such as 'Since all the above terms are at least 0, we get that Thus,' appear repeatedly. These reduce confidence in the overall proofreading.

The central open question for the frequency-prediction setting (whether EF1 is achievable for n >= 3, or whether even a positive approximation is possible) is left unresolved (Section 5, end), leaving a noticeable hole in the characterization: the paper gives EFX for n = 2 and a 0-approximation for EFX for n >= 3, but nothing about the weaker and arguably most natural notion EF1 in between.

The claim in Theorem 4.3 for n >= 3 is established only by reference to the proof of Theorem 6.4, which assumes identical valuations (a special case). While logically sufficient for an impossibility, the asymmetric reliance on a restricted setting is never explicitly justified in the text and may confuse readers about the generality of the result.

No empirical component or illustrative experiments are provided to gauge how the proposed algorithms behave on realistic instances or how much normalization/frequency information actually matters in practice; the paper is purely worst-case theoretical, which is acceptable for the venue but limits demonstrated impact.

There is no explicit limitations or ethics discussion; the limitations are scattered through the text (open problems, conjecture in Section 5, robustness deferred in the conclusion) rather than consolidated, which weakens the treatment of the scope of the claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and natural question—how the availability of information about future goods affects the satisfiability of classic fairness notions in online fair division—and organizes the answer cleanly across four information regimes (none, normalization, frequency predictions, identical valuations).

The meta-theorem (Theorem 5.1) is the highlight: the constructive reduction showing that any share-based fairness notion achievable offline can be matched online using frequency predictions is elegant, general, and immediately transfers state-of-the-art offline guarantees (e.g., (3/4 + 3/3836)-MMS via Akrami and Garg) to the online setting, improving on the tight 0.5-MMS bound under normalization alone.
The tight characterization for two agents with identical valuations and normalization (Theorem 6.3) with a matching (√5−1)/2-EFX algorithm and impossibility is a nice, complete result.
The paper usefully corrects an error in the proof of Kahana and Hazon [2023] (Example 3.2), which serves the community.

Impossibility results (Proposition 3.1, Theorems 4.3, 4.4, 5.6, 6.4) are strong (zero competitive ratio) and are proved with explicit adversarial constructions; the write-up includes detailed proofs for most claims, supporting verifiability.

The related work section is thorough and positions the contribution accurately relative to learning-augmented approaches, semi-online scheduling, and online fair division, honestly noting what is known versus new (e.g., reproducing Elkind et al.'s EF1 result for identical valuations 'for completeness').
weaknesses: Several results are incremental over prior work: the normalization-setting algorithm (Algorithm 1) is explicitly a generalization/modification of Zhou et al. [2023], and its guarantees (EF1/0.5-MMS for n=2, PROP1 for any n) are modest; Proposition 6.1 is a reproduction of a known result. The genuinely new technical content is concentrated in Section 5.

The frequency prediction model is a very strong informational assumption: the algorithm is given the exact multiset of all future valuations per agent (equivalently, the exact number of items and each value). This is nearly 'offline information except order,' which limits practical applicability; robustness to noisy or partial predictions is deferred to future work, so the model sits awkwardly between the common normalization assumption and full offline knowledge.

The central question for the frequency-prediction setting is left unresolved: whether EF1 (or a positive approximation) is achievable for n ≥ 3 remains open (Section 5), so the fairness picture in the strongest information regime is incomplete.

There are noticeable proof and presentation errors that, while seemingly fixable, reduce confidence: in Theorem 4.4, Case 2 concludes 'as δ → 0' where δ → ∞ is meant; in Theorem 5.5 the definition of B2 contains a typo ({f(g) | g ∈ A2 \ {f(g*)}} should use g*); Algorithm 3's caption renders the (√5−1)/2 constant incorrectly; Theorem 4.3's n ≥ 3 case is handled by referral to Theorem 6.4's proof, which assumes identical valuations—valid but confusingly structured.

The impossibility proofs largely follow the standard adversary-presentation style of Zhou et al. and Benadè et al., so their technical novelty is limited; the competitive-ratio framework for fairness properties is inherited rather than newly developed.
No empirical evaluation, which is acceptable for a theory contribution but means the practical relevance of, e.g., frequency predictions or the (√5−1)/2-EFX algorithm is untested.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic study: the paper cleanly organizes the landscape of online fair division for indivisible goods across three information models (none, normalization information, frequency predictions), and Table 1 gives a clear at-a-glance summary of what is and is not achievable, including honest '?' entries for open cases.

Strong and largely tight technical results: the PROP1 algorithm under normalization information (Theorem 4.2) is the first satisfiable fairness guarantee for n>=3 in this setting; the impossibility results (Theorems 4.3, 4.4, 5.6, 6.4) are carefully constructed; and Theorem 6.3 achieves a matching upper and lower bound of (sqrt(5)-1)/2 for EFX with two agents under identical valuations and normalization information, which is a particularly clean and complete contribution.

The general meta-algorithm (Theorem 5.1) is elegant and broadly useful: it shows that ANY feasible share-based fairness notion in the single-shot setting can be lifted to the online setting via frequency predictions, immediately implying the best-known (3/4 + 3/3836)-MMS guarantee online for any number of agents, improving on the prior 0.5-MMS result. The proof via IDO (identically ordered) instances and picking sequences is clean and reusable.

The learning-augmented variants (Theorems 4.5 and 5.7) are well-motivated and yield graceful degradation: multiplicative kappa-PROP1 under noisy totals and (1-eps)-share guarantees under noisy frequency predictions, with a concrete instantiation rule and an honest appendix (Example B.1) clarifying why EF1 robustness is inherently additive rather than multiplicative.

Scholarly value beyond the main results: the paper identifies and corrects a flaw in the Kahana and Hazon [2023] impossibility construction (Example 3.2/Corollary 3.4), and properly extends deterministic lower bounds to randomized algorithms under the adaptive-adversary ex-post model (Appendix A) with a clear statement of the pathwise guarantee notion.

Presentation is generally clear and self-contained; preliminaries are precise, algorithms are described intuitively alongside pseudocode, and the related-work section situates the contribution well against online scheduling with advice, learning-augmented allocation, and bandit-based fair division. Practical motivation (compute slots, content moderation, food banks) is convincingly argued.
weaknesses: Incremental positioning relative to Zhou et al. [2023]: Algorithm 1 is explicitly a generalization/modification of their 0.5-MMS algorithm, and several impossibility results build directly on prior lower bounds (Benade et al. [2018]). While the new guarantees (EF1 for n=2, PROP1 for all n) are genuine advances, the core algorithmic template is inherited rather than new.

The frequency-predictions model is strong in a specific sense: it assumes exact multiset knowledge including the total number of goods m, and guarantees are worst-case over adversarial permutations of the known values. This is a natural semi-online formalization, but its applicability to realistic predictive pipelines rests mostly on the noisy variants, where the instantiation-error parameter eta_i couples prediction quality with the online instantiation rule in a way that is discussed but not tightly characterized (bounding eta_i in terms of multiset distance is left open).

Some central questions remain unresolved and are only flagged: EF1 with frequency predictions for n>=3 is left open with a conjecture of impossibility, and positive approximate EF1/EFX guarantees under noisy normalization for n>=3 are not explored. This limits the completeness of the information-model taxonomy the paper sets up.

The results are purely worst-case/ex-post and deterministic in the main body; the treatment of randomized algorithms (Appendix A) is correct but the pathwise ex-post notion is very strong, so the impossibility results for randomization may be less informative than they appear for readers used to ex-ante or oblivious-adversary models. The paper acknowledges this but does not develop the weaker-adversary variants.

Minor presentation issues: some impossibility proofs (e.g., Theorems 4.3 and 6.3) are long case analyses with many magic constants (2^{-k^2}, k = ceil((sqrt(5)-2)/eps)) that are hard to absorb; a few statements (e.g., Corollary 3.4's reliance on the adaptive adversary generating the Benade et al. instance) deserve slightly more justification. There are also minor typographical/notation slips (e.g., 'other agent from N\{1}' in Theorem 5.6's proof, question marks in Table 1 for EF1 under frequency predictions with n>=3).

strengths: The paper presents a systematic and well-organized study of how different levels of future information (none, normalization/totals, frequency multisets) affect the achievability of standard fairness notions (EF1/EFX/PROP1/MMS) in online fair division under an adaptive adversary with ex post guarantees. The information hierarchy is a clean and useful conceptual framing.

The results are nearly complete for the EF1/PROP1/EFX landscape: tight matching upper and lower bounds are given in several regimes (e.g., EFX under identical valuations with normalization information in Theorem 6.3 is tight; EFX impossibility even with frequency predictions for n >= 3 in Theorem 5.6).

Theorem 5.1 is the strongest technical contribution: a constructive meta-algorithm showing that any feasible share in the single-shot setting can be lifted to the online setting with frequency predictions, immediately yielding the best-known MMS approximation (3/4 + 3/3836) online for any number of agents, improving on the 0.5-MMS bound of Zhou et al. [2023].

The learning-augmented variants (Theorems 4.5 and 5.7) degrade gracefully with explicit error parameters, and Appendix B honestly analyzes the gap between additive (EF1) and multiplicative (PROP1) robustness, including a counterexample showing no multiplicative EF1 guarantee is possible under noisy advice.

The paper corrects a flaw in the impossibility construction of Kahana and Hazon [2023] (Example 3.2) and strengthens prior impossibilities (Proposition 3.1 shows no positive EF1 approximation without information), which is a genuine service to the community.

Proofs are careful and self-contained, algorithms are simple and implementable in polynomial time (O(mn) for Algorithm 1, O(m^2 n) for Algorithm 2), and the related-work coverage is thorough and positions the contribution accurately (including the distinction from divisible-goods learning-augmented work and bandit-feedback settings).
weaknesses: Algorithm 1 is an explicit modification of Zhou et al. [2023, Algorithm 1], and several results build directly on their techniques and lower bounds; the novelty of the normalization-information section (Section 4) is somewhat incremental relative to that prior work, with the main new elements being the EF1/PROP1 guarantees and the flaw correction.

Section 6 partly reproduces known results (Proposition 6.1 is a reproduction of Elkind et al. [2025a, Thm 3.7]) and its motivation as a scheduling benchmark is somewhat peripheral to the main narrative.

The learning-augmented analysis under noisy frequency predictions (Theorem 5.7) treats the instantiation error eta_i as an end-to-end parameter but does not bound it in terms of a natural predictor-quality measure; the authors acknowledge this, but it leaves the practical relevance of the robustness result somewhat open. Similarly, the certified-interval advice model for totals is a strong assumption.

Some assumptions deserve scrutiny: frequency predictions require knowing the exact number of goods m in advance and reveal each agent's multiset of future values, which is quite strong information; the model justification via 'type' forecasting is plausible but the worst-case adversarial-permutation semantics could be stated with more care.

The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical evaluation, and a couple of natural questions are left open (e.g., EF1 for n >= 3 with frequency predictions is only conjectured to be impossible), though the authors are transparent about this.

Minor presentation issues: some impossibility proofs (Theorems 4.3, 4.4, 6.3) are long and case-heavy with many parameter choices, which can be hard to follow; a few claimed tightness statements rely on limits that are verified only asymptotically.
